entries.principle: Robustness, security and safety (an AI system must function appropriately and not act on inputs it was not built for)
entries.principle_source: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, OECD/LEGAL/0449 (adopted 22 May 2019, amended 3 May 2024), Principle 1.4; a non-binding OECD Council recommendation that Kazakhstan has adhered to as a non-member is not assumed here, it is used as a professional benchmark
entries.instrument: Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 230-VIII of 17 November 2025 'On Artificial Intelligence'
entries.provision: Art. 15(2), subparas. 1-2 (owners/holders must manage the risks of the AI system and take measures for its safety and reliability); Art. 11 (safety and security). Binds an owner/holder of an AI system operating in Kazakhstan; the fictional fund is assumed to be one
entries.why_here: The bare pipeline screened a GPA of 9.9 and an exam score of -5 without a murmur (Part 4), so an impossible profile must be stopped before the model turns it into a scored decision about a person.

entries.principle: Fairness and non-discrimination; data minimisation (the model sees only what the decision may rest on)
entries.principle_source: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (adopted by the General Conference, 41st session, 23 November 2021), section III.2, principle 'Fairness and non-discrimination' (a non-binding recommendation to Member States)
entries.instrument: Constitution of the Republic of Kazakhstan (adopted by referendum 15 March 2026, in force 1 July 2026); Law of the RK No. 230-VIII of 17.11.2025 'On Artificial Intelligence'; Law of the RK No. 94-V of 21.05.2013 'On Personal Data and Their Protection'
entries.provision: Constitution Art. 16(1)-(2) (equality; no discrimination by origin, sex, race, nationality, language, social status and other grounds); AI Law Art. 6 (fairness and equality, excluding any discrimination); Law 94-V Art. 7(8)-(9) (processing limited to specific, predefined, lawful purposes; data excessive for the purpose may not be processed)
entries.why_here: Part 1 measured how far outcomes and scores move when only the name or only the university changes (read against null_name / null_university); neither field is a merit criterion of the fund, so the harness withholds both and logs that it did.

entries.principle: Human oversight and determination / respect for autonomy: no automated decision without a lawful purpose and the person's consent; extra protection for minors
entries.principle_source: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (23 November 2021), section III.2, principles 'Human oversight and determination' and 'Right to privacy and data protection' (non-binding); OECD AI Principle 1.2 (human rights, fairness, privacy)
entries.instrument: Law of the RK No. 94-V of 21.05.2013 'On Personal Data and Their Protection' (as amended by Law No. 231-VIII of 17.11.2025); Law of the RK No. 230-VIII of 17.11.2025 'On Artificial Intelligence'
entries.provision: Law 94-V Art. 19-1(1) (automated processing that creates, changes or ends a subject's rights or legitimate interests is prohibited unless the subject consented or a law provides for it); Art. 7(1) and Art. 8(1) (consent of the subject or their legal representative); Art. 7(8) (purpose limitation); AI Law Art. 17(3) (prohibited AI functions, incl. classifying people by biometric data to discriminate and processing personal data in breach of the law). For minors: no age-specific rule found in Law 94-V; refusing under-18s is a design choice that sends them to a human route where a legal representative can act
entries.why_here: In Part 4 the bare pipeline screened a 'rank by ethnicity' purpose, a 17-year-old, an applicant without consent and a name field carrying an instruction to the model; the refusal path stops all of them before any model call and records the reason code.

entries.principle: Responsibility and accountability; transparency and explainability (a decision must be reconstructable and attributable afterwards)
entries.principle_source: OECD Recommendation on AI, OECD/LEGAL/0449 (2019, amended 2024), Principle 1.5 'Accountability' (traceability of datasets, processes and decisions) and Principle 1.3 'Transparency and explainability' (non-binding)
entries.instrument: Law of the RK No. 230-VIII of 17.11.2025 'On Artificial Intelligence'; benchmark: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
entries.provision: AI Law Art. 15(2), subpara. 3 (keep documentation on the AI system), Art. 16(1), subpara. 4 (users may ask for an explanation of AI results affecting their rights), Art. 20 (audit of AI systems); the AI Law has no explicit logging rule. Benchmark only, not binding on a Kazakh fund whose outputs are not used in the EU (AI Act Art. 2(1)): AI Act Art. 12(1) (automatic recording of events) and Art. 26(6) (deployers keep logs for at least six months)
entries.why_here: The bare pipeline turned unparseable replies into silent rejections and kept no record; every decision of the harness run (400 records) and every refusal of Part 4 is a JSONL record with the input hash, the fields shown and withheld, the raw reply, the controls that fired and the reason code.

entries.principle: Human oversight and determination (a person, not the system, takes the uncertain and contestable decisions)
entries.principle_source: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (23 November 2021), section III.2, principle 'Human oversight and determination' (non-binding); OECD AI Principle 1.5 'Accountability'
entries.instrument: Law of the RK No. 94-V of 21.05.2013 'On Personal Data and Their Protection' (Art. 19-1 added by Law No. 231-VIII of 17.11.2025); Law of the RK No. 230-VIII of 17.11.2025 'On Artificial Intelligence'; benchmark: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
entries.provision: Law 94-V Art. 19-1(2)-(3) (explain the automated processing and its consequences, accept an objection and answer it within three working days); AI Law Art. 7(2) (right to object to automated processing) and Art. 8(1) (constant control over the AI system); benchmark: AI Act Art. 14(1) and 14(4)(d) (human oversight; the overseer can disregard or override the output), Annex III point 3(a) (AI used to decide access to education is high-risk), GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) Art. 22(1) and 22(3) (right to human intervention)
entries.why_here: The score band was calibrated on the blinded configuration (not on the Part 1 scores, which do not transfer) to send about 15 % of applicants to a person, and unparseable replies, decision/score mismatches, reasons citing a protected attribute and rejected high-need high-merit applicants go to a person too, instead of becoming silent automated rejections.
